I’m an applied sociologist and quantitative social scientist interested in how social inequalities shape people’s life chances and the societies they live in. My work combines substantive sociological questions with empirical analysis, particularly around social inequality, migration, diversity, trust, and social cohesion.

I work mainly with quantitative and internationally comparative data, including survey and longitudinal data, to examine how inequalities emerge, persist, and vary across institutional and national contexts. More recently, my work has expanded into child and youth wellbeing, health inequalities, disability, and institutional access: when do institutions reproduce existing disadvantages, and when can they help to offset them?

I also have a strong interest in open science, reproducible research, data harmonisation, and research infrastructure. These interests shape how I approach empirical work, with an emphasis on transparent and well-documented workflows that make data and analytical decisions easier to understand, verify, and reuse.

In recent years, my work has increasingly combined research with research coordination and project development, particularly in international and interdisciplinary settings.
